summary: Defines the ipp: URL scheme, used to give the network location of a print service that speaks the Internet Printing Protocol, or of a printer or other resource it manages. It expands and clarifies the IPP URL section of RFC 2910. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Every printer on a network needs an address so computers can find it. This memo says how to write that address so it clearly points to a printer that understands the Internet Printing Protocol.

questions: how to write an ipp printer address
subtitle: The exact rules for writing ipp: addresses that point to network printers and print jobs.

tldr.problem: IPP clients need a clear, uniform way to name a print service or a print job. The short IPP URL section in RFC 2910 left gaps.
tldr.mechanism: The ipp: URL scheme borrows HTTP URL syntax, defaults to port 631, and comes with comparison rules and conformance requirements for clients and printers.
tldr.outcome: It adds no new URL parameters. It expands and clarifies the IPP URL section of RFC 2910, which it updates, and registers the scheme.

today: RFC 3510 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 2910, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Separate IPP URL Memo
sections.content:
This memo defines the ipp URL scheme. An ipp: URL names the network location of a print service that speaks the Internet Printing Protocol, or of a resource that such a service manages, for example a print job.

It updates RFC 2910 by expanding and clarifying that RFC's Section 5, "IPP URL Scheme". It does not define any new parameters or other extensions to the syntax of IPP URLs. It also follows the URL scheme registration rules in RFC 2717 and the guidelines in RFC 2718.
sections.eli5: An earlier document gave printer addresses only a short description. This one fills in the details without changing how the addresses look.

sections.title: Printers, Jobs and What a URL Points To
sections.content:
The memo reuses the object model of RFC 2911. An IPP Client is software that submits, monitors or manages print jobs. An IPP Printer is software that receives jobs and operations from a client. It might front a spooler, a gateway or a physical printing device. An IPP Job is the set of attributes and documents for one print job on a Printer.

The ipp: scheme may only be used for absolute URLs, so relative IPP URLs are not allowed. It means the abstract IPP protocol carried over an HTTP transport, as defined in RFC 2910. Any other transport binding would need a different URL scheme. A client can use an IPP URL, perhaps found in a directory, to open an HTTP connection to the print service and send requests such as Print-Job.
sections.eli5: A printer is the thing that takes in print requests, and a job is one request waiting or running on it. The address says which printer you are talking to.

sections.title: Syntax, Port and Encoding
sections.content:
The syntax in ABNF is ipp-URL = "ipp:" "//" host [ ":" port ] [ abs_path [ "?" query ]]. It is based on the HTTP URL syntax, which comes from the generic URI syntax of RFC 2396 and was updated for IPv6 by RFC 2732.

If the port is empty or not given, port 631 is assumed. That is the IANA-assigned well-known port. The resource is the one located at the IPP print service listening for HTTP connections on that port of that host. The Request-URI is the abs_path, and when no abs_path is present it MUST be given as /.

IPP URLs MUST use RFC 2396 encoding, as their equivalent HTTP URLs do. All IPP URLs MUST be used to specify print services that support the application/ipp MIME media type for requests and responses.

The IPP model limits a URI to 1023 octets (not characters). The memo adds that printers ought to be cautious about relying on lengths above 255 bytes, because some older clients might not handle them.
sections.eli5: An IPP address is like a web address that starts with ipp:. If you leave off the door number, the computer knocks on door 631, the usual printing door.

sections.title: Examples, Job URLs and Comparison
sections.content:
Printer URLs such as ipp://example.com/printer/tiger and ipp://example.com/printer/tiger/bob each reference a logically different IPP Printer, even if they share a host. A last path component might name a physical device, a group such as a load-balancing spooler, or a separate job queue on one device. The memo says literal IPv4 or IPv6 addresses SHOULD NOT be used in IPP URLs.

For Jobs, RFC 2911 says the format of a Job URI is implementation dependent. The memo points out that the claimed way to get from a job URL back to its Printer URL is actually unspecified. To help interoperability, conforming Printers SHOULD generate a Job URL by appending exactly one path component to the Printer URL, as in ipp://example.com/printer/123. Job URLs are valid only until the job completes, plus any optional period the implementation keeps them.

To compare two IPP URLs, a client MUST use the HTTP URI comparison rules of RFC 2616 with one exception: an empty or missing port is treated as equivalent to port 631. So ipp://example.com/~smith/printer and ipp://example.com:631/~smith/printer are equivalent.
sections.eli5: Two addresses can look different but mean the same printer, such as one with the usual door number written out and one without. The rules say to treat those as the same.

sections.title: Rules for Clients and Printers
sections.content:
A conforming client MUST connect only to the port in the IPP URL, or to port 631 if none is given. It MUST send only URLs that match the ABNF in outgoing requests. It MUST convert IPP URLs to HTTP URL form only by the rules in Section 5 of RFC 2910.

A conforming Printer MUST listen on port 631 unless administrators or site policy configure otherwise, and SHOULD NOT listen on any other port unless explicitly configured. It SHOULD accept and send only URLs that match the ABNF, SHOULD build Job URLs by appending one path component, and SHOULD NOT use literal IPv4 or IPv6 addresses in configured or locally generated IPP URLs.
sections.eli5: Clients must knock on the right door and write addresses the proper way. Printers must stay by door 631 unless someone tells them to move.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo adds no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 2910 and RFC 2911, except four points. A URL might be faked to point to a rogue print service that collects confidential document contents. A URL might be used by an unauthorized client. A URL might lead to a gateway, for example an IPP to LPD gateway, which silently compromises IPP security, and the memo says a client has no practical defense against this. Finally, an IPP URL carries no parameters naming the required authentication or security mechanism, so discovery or directory protocols might be used to learn them.

The first two threats are said to be addressed by the server and client authentication and security mechanisms in RFC 2910. The working group chose not to add such parameters, for backward compatibility with many shipping IPP/1.1 implementations.
sections.eli5: Someone could trick you into sending your document to a fake printer, so the existing security tools matter. The address itself does not say which tools a printer needs.
